title: The Late Period
subtitle: 664–332 BC · The Saite Renaissance, the Persian Conquests and the Last Pharaohs

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From Psamtik I's reunification and the Saite renaissance through two Persian conquests and the last native pharaohs to Alexander

entries.label: Psamtik I — reunification from Sais
entries.hint: Installed as a local vassal by Assyria after the sack of Thebes, Psamtik I built up his own power in the western Delta, hired Ionian and Carian mercenaries — Herodotus's 'bronze men from the sea' — bought off or absorbed the other Delta princes, and by about 656 controlled all Egypt. He secured Thebes without a fight by having his daughter Nitocris adopted as the next God's Wife of Amun. His 54-year reign restored a single Egyptian state after four centuries of division.
entries.note: Nitocris Adoption Stela (Cairo JE 36327), 656 BC. Herodotus 2.151–54. Alan B. Lloyd, 'The Late Period', in Shaw (ed.), Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) pp.369–79; Anthony Spalinger, 'Psammetichus, King of Egypt I', JARCE 13 (1976).

entries.label: Necho II — Carchemish and the canal
entries.hint: Necho II marched north to shore up the collapsing Assyrian empire against Babylon — killing King Josiah of Judah at Megiddo on the way — and held Syria briefly before Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed his army at Carchemish in 605 and drove Egypt out of the Levant for good. At home he began digging a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, built a fleet of Greek-style triremes, and, Herodotus says, sent a Phoenician crew to sail around Africa.
entries.note: Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 5) for Carchemish; 2 Kings 23:29, Jeremiah 46. Herodotus 2.158–59 (canal, triremes), 4.42 (circumnavigation). Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.371–72.

entries.label: Psamtik II — the raid into Kush
entries.hint: Psamtik II's short reign is remembered for a single campaign: in 593 his army, stiffened with Greek, Carian and Phoenician mercenaries, drove deep into the Kushite kingdom, perhaps as far as Napata, and came home with prisoners and loot. Soldiers scratched their names on the leg of a colossus at Abu Simbel — among the oldest Greek inscriptions anywhere. The blow helped push the Kushite centre of gravity south toward Meroe, and Psamtik had Kushite royal names hacked from Egyptian monuments.
entries.note: Abu Simbel mercenary graffiti: Meiggs & Lewis, A Selection of Greek Historical Inscriptions (1969) no.7. Kush campaign: the Tanis, Karnak and Shellal stelae; Robert Morkot, The Black Pharaohs (2000) pp.296–98; László Török, The Kingdom of Kush (1997) pp.362–69.

entries.label: Apries — the king the army overthrew
entries.hint: Apries — the 'Pharaoh Hophra' of the book of Jeremiah — encouraged Judah to rebel against Babylon and could not save Jerusalem when it fell in 587. He campaigned by sea against Tyre and Sidon, but when an Egyptian army he sent to help settlers against the Greek city of Cyrene was cut to pieces in 570, the native troops mutinied, believing he had spent them to weaken them. His general Amasis was proclaimed king; Apries was captured and killed in 567.
entries.note: Jeremiah 44:30, 37:5–11. Cyrene disaster and mutiny: Herodotus 2.161–63, 169. Amasis stela (Elephantine): translation in Lloyd, Herodotus Book II: Commentary 99–182 (1988). Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.372–74.

entries.label: Amasis — forty-four years of prosperity
entries.hint: Amasis, a soldier of common birth, reigned longer than any Saite king in wealth and peace. He concentrated the Greek traders of Egypt at the single port of Naukratis and taxed them, married a woman of Cyrene, sent gifts to Greek temples, and knitted an anti-Persian network with Lydia, Babylon, Sparta and the tyrant Polycrates of Samos. Herodotus tells him as a shrewd, unbuttoned figure — hearing cases in the morning and drinking in the afternoon — and rates his reign Egypt's most prosperous.
entries.note: Herodotus 2.172–82, 3.10–16. Naukratis regulation: Herodotus 2.178–79; Astrid Möller, Naukratis: Trade in Archaic Greece (2000). Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.374–76.

entries.label: Psamtik III — six months and the fall
entries.hint: Psamtik III had ruled barely half a year when Cambyses II of Persia invaded. The Egyptian army, its Greek mercenaries partly bought away by a defector, was beaten at Pelusium on the eastern frontier and fell back on Memphis, which was besieged and stormed. Psamtik III was taken to the Persian court, and executed after being implicated in a revolt. The Twenty-sixth Dynasty and Egyptian independence ended together.
entries.note: Herodotus 3.10–15. The mercenary defector Phanes of Halicarnassus: Herodotus 3.4. Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002) pp.52–55.

entries.label: Cambyses II — Egypt becomes a Persian province
entries.hint: Cambyses ruled Egypt as an Egyptian king, taking a pharaonic titulary and, if the courtier Udjahorresnet is to be believed, being coached in Egyptian protocol and expelling foreign squatters from a Saite temple. Later Egyptian and Greek tradition made him a mad sacrilege — stabbing the Apis bull, burning mummies, losing an army in the desert on the way to Siwa — but a contemporary Apis burial dated to his reign shows the bull story is at least exaggerated.
entries.note: Statue of Udjahorresnet (Vatican 22690): Alan B. Lloyd, 'The Inscription of Udjahorresnet', JEA 68 (1982). The Apis stela dated to Cambyses' Year 6 (Louvre): contra Herodotus 3.27–29. The lost army toward Siwa: Herodotus 3.26. Briant (2002) pp.55–61.

entries.label: Darius I — the canal, the law code and Hibis
entries.hint: Darius I governed Egypt through a conciliatory policy: he completed the Nile–Red Sea canal Necho had started, marking it with granite stelae in Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian and Egyptian; he ordered scholars to compile the laws of Egypt down to the reign of Amasis; and he built the temple of Amun at Hibis in the Kharga Oasis, one of the few temples any Persian king raised. Assessed Egyptian tribute was heavy, and a revolt broke out as he died.
entries.note: Suez canal stelae of Darius: Posener, La première domination perse en Égypte (1936). Law codification: the verso of the Demotic Chronicle (P. BN 215). Hibis temple: Norman de Garis Davies, The Temple of Hibis in El Khārgeh Oasis (1953). Briant (2002) pp.472–84.

entries.label: Xerxes I to Artaxerxes I — revolt and reconquest
entries.hint: Xerxes I put down the revolt of 486 hard and, Herodotus says, treated Egypt more harshly than his father had. The great rising of Inaros of the western Delta from about 460, backed by a large Athenian fleet, held most of Lower Egypt for years before the Persian general Megabyzus crushed it and trapped the Athenians in the marshes. When Herodotus toured Egypt around 450 he found it a Persian province again, and gathered the material for Book Two of his Histories.
entries.note: Herodotus 7.7 (Xerxes), 3.12, 3.15 (Inaros). Thucydides 1.104, 1.109–10 (the Athenian expedition). Herodotus's visit: Alan B. Lloyd, Herodotus Book II: Introduction (1975).

entries.label: Darius II and the end of the first occupation
entries.hint: Under Darius II Persian control loosened. The Aramaic papyri of the Jewish military colony on Elephantine island date mostly to these years — legal deeds, letters, and a request to the Persian and Judaean authorities to rebuild their temple to Yahu, destroyed by a mob with local Egyptian priests' backing in 410. Around 404, as Darius II died and Persia fell into a succession war, Amyrtaeus of Sais led a revolt that made Egypt independent again.
entries.note: Elephantine papyri: Bezalel Porten & Ada Yardeni, Textbook of Aramaic Documents from Ancient Egypt (1986–99); Porten, Archives from Elephantine (1968). The temple-rebuilding petition: TAD A4.7–9. Briant (2002) pp.588–91.

entries.label: Amyrtaeus — the one-king dynasty
entries.hint: Amyrtaeus of Sais, grandson of a leader of an earlier revolt, drove the last Persian garrison out of Egypt and ruled as the sole king of the Twenty-eighth Dynasty, recognised as far south as Aswan by 400. After five years he was defeated and executed — an Aramaic papyrus from Elephantine records the event and the accession of 'Nepherites, king' — and power passed to a rival family from Mendes.
entries.note: Aramaic Papyrus Brooklyn 47.218.152 (the 'Amyrtaeus' papyrus): recording his death 'according to law' and Nepherites' accession. Kienitz, Die politische Geschichte Ägyptens vom 7. bis zum 4. Jahrhundert vor der Zeitwende (1953).

entries.label: Nepherites I and Hakor — independence held with Greek help
entries.hint: The Twenty-ninth Dynasty, from Mendes, kept Egypt free through diplomacy and hired soldiers. Nepherites I allied with Sparta against Persia; his successor Hakor (Achoris) switched to Athens and Evagoras of Cyprus, hired the Athenian general Chabrias, built extensively across Egypt, and beat off a Persian attempt around 385–383. The dynasty ended in a coup after his death, with the throne seized by a general from Sebennytos.
entries.note: Diodorus 14.79, 15.2–4, 15.8–9. Hakor's building: monuments at Karnak, Medinet Habu, Tell el-Maskhuta. Kienitz (1953); Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.377–79.

entries.label: Nectanebo I — the invasion of 373 turned back
entries.hint: Nectanebo I of Sebennytos founded the Thirtieth Dynasty and, in 373, faced the largest Persian effort yet — a fleet and army under Pharnabazus with the Athenian Iphicrates commanding the Greek troops. The Persians forced the Mendesian mouth of the Nile but hesitated, quarrelled, and were caught by the rising flood; they withdrew without taking Memphis. Nectanebo I then poured resources into temple-building on a scale not seen since the New Kingdom.
entries.note: Diodorus 15.41–43. The invasion and its failure: John Ray, 'Egypt 525–404 B.C.' and 'Egypt: Dependence and Independence', in Cambridge Ancient History IV and VI (1988–94). Naukratis (Thonis-Heracleion) Decree of Nectanebo I: Franck Goddio's underwater find, 2000.

entries.label: Teos — the offensive that broke on its own cost
entries.hint: Teos took the war to Persia, leading an army into Phoenicia with Greek mercenaries under the aged Spartan king Agesilaus and the Athenian Chabrias. To pay them he taxed the temples and the people heavily and seized temple treasure, which turned opinion against him at home. His own family engineered a coup during the campaign, proclaiming his nephew Nectanebo; Teos fled to the Persian court he had come to fight.
entries.note: Plutarch, Agesilaus 36–40; Xenophon, Agesilaus 2.28–31; Diodorus 15.92–93. Teos's fiscal measures: [Aristotle], Oeconomica 2.2.25a. Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.379–80.

entries.label: Nectanebo II — the last pharaoh
entries.hint: Nectanebo II ruled eighteen years, the last Egyptian to hold the throne. He built or added to temples the length of the country, poured patronage into the animal cults, and in 351 turned back a Persian invasion. When Artaxerxes III came again in 343 with a larger force and Greek generals, Nectanebo's defence of the Delta collapsed; he withdrew upriver with the treasury and disappeared, probably into Nubia. Later legend, in the Alexander Romance, made him a magician who fathered Alexander the Great.
entries.note: Diodorus 16.40–51. Building record: the largest of any Late Period king; the Nectanebo II sphinx avenue at Saqqara, the Karnak first pylon. Alexander Romance I.1–14. Ian Moyer, Egypt and the Limits of Hellenism (2011) on the later legend.

entries.label: Artaxerxes III to Mazaces — reconquest and surrender
entries.hint: Artaxerxes III's reconquest in 343 was remembered as a brutal one — walls thrown down, temples plundered, sacred records carried off, and a revived tale of a Persian king killing the Apis. Egypt was a satrapy again for eleven years under a run of governors. The last of them, Mazaces, having no army after the Persian defeat at Issus, handed Egypt to Alexander the Great in 332 without a fight; Alexander sacrificed to the Apis, was crowned at Memphis, and founded Alexandria.
entries.note: Diodorus 16.46–51 (reconquest), 17.49 (Alexander's arrival); Arrian, Anabasis 3.1–5; [Aristotle] Oeconomica 2.2.33–35. Briant (2002) pp.681–90, 1017–19. Alexander at Siwa: Arrian 3.3–4.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The battles of Carchemish and Pelusium, the Nubian campaign, and the wars to keep Persia out of the Nile

entries.label: The end of the Kushite claim
entries.hint: Assyria's withdrawal left Egypt to be reassembled. Psamtik I did it by a mix of force, subsidy and marriage-diplomacy: he neutralised the Delta princes, garrisoned the frontiers with Ionian and Carian troops settled in camps at the Pelusiac mouth, and in 656 secured Thebes bloodlessly through his daughter Nitocris's adoption as heir to the God's Wife of Amun. When Tantamani of Kush died in 653 the Twenty-fifth Dynasty's claim on Egypt died with him.
entries.note: Nitocris Adoption Stela (Cairo JE 36327). The mercenary camps ('the Stratopeda'): Herodotus 2.154. Anthony Spalinger, 'The Concept of the Monarchy during the Saite Epoch', Orientalia 47 (1978).

entries.label: Megiddo and the death of Josiah
entries.hint: When the last Assyrian forces made their stand against Babylon at Harran, Necho II marched an Egyptian army north to help them. King Josiah of Judah moved to block the pass at Megiddo and was killed there, an event the books of Kings and Chronicles treat as a national catastrophe. Necho pressed on, imposed a tribute on Judah and installed a client king, and held the Levant as far as the Euphrates for four years.
entries.note: 2 Kings 23:29–35; 2 Chronicles 35:20–24; Jeremiah 22:10–12. Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3–4. Nadav Na'aman, 'The Kingdom of Judah under Josiah', Tel Aviv 18 (1991).

entries.label: The Battle of Carchemish
entries.hint: At Carchemish the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Necho II's field army and pursued the survivors south; a follow-up victory at Hamath finished the campaign. Egypt lost Syria and Palestine permanently and never again projected land power beyond Sinai except as a raider. The Babylonian Chronicle's terse account — the Egyptian army 'withdrew before him' and 'was beaten and could not escape' — marks the end of Egypt as a great power in the Near East.
entries.note: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 5 (BM 21946); Jeremiah 46:2–12. D.J. Wiseman, Chronicles of Chaldaean Kings (1956); Israel Ephʿal, The City Besieged (2009).

entries.label: Psamtik II's expedition into Kush
entries.hint: In his third year Psamtik II sent an army under the general Potasimto and the Egyptian commander Amasis, its ranks full of Greek, Carian and Phoenician mercenaries, up the Nile against Kush. It defeated a Kushite force and raided deep — a stela claims the taking of a place read as Pnubs or beyond, near Napata. Homesick soldiers cut their names into a colossus at Abu Simbel. The raid did no lasting damage but confirmed the Kushite retreat toward Meroe.
entries.note: Karnak, Tanis and Shellal stelae of Psamtik II: Sauneron & Yoyotte, 'La campagne nubienne de Psammétique II', BIFAO 50 (1952). Abu Simbel graffiti: Meiggs & Lewis, GHI no.7.

entries.label: The Battle of Pelusium
entries.hint: Cambyses II crossed Sinai with Arab help arranging water in the desert, and met the Egyptian army under Psamtik III at Pelusium, the fortress guarding the eastern approach. The Egyptians were beaten and fell back on Memphis, which surrendered after a siege. Herodotus, who saw the battlefield, reports the bones of the two armies still lying separate decades later, and tells a story of Cambyses driving cats and other sacred animals before his troops so the Egyptians would not shoot.
entries.note: Herodotus 3.10–13. Polyaenus 7.9 (the animal-shields story). Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002) pp.52–55.

entries.label: The revolt of Inaros
entries.loc: Memphis (the White Castle) / the Delta marshes
entries.hint: Inaros, a Libyan dynast of the western Delta, raised most of Lower Egypt against Persia and called in Athens, then at war with Persia, which sent about two hundred ships. The rebels beat a Persian army, killed the satrap Achaemenes, and penned the survivors in the fortified quarter of Memphis for eighteen months. The Persian general Megabyzus broke the siege, drove the Athenians onto an island in the Nile and forced their surrender; a relief squadron was ambushed. Inaros was crucified.
entries.note: Thucydides 1.104, 1.109–10; Herodotus 3.12, 3.15; Ctesias, Persica F14. Analysis: Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002) pp.573–77; Kahn, 'Inaros' Rebellion against Artaxerxes I', Classical Quarterly 58 (2008).

entries.label: The invasion of 373 BC repelled
entries.loc: the Mendesian mouth of the Nile
entries.hint: After decades of failed attempts, Persia sent its largest force yet against independent Egypt: perhaps 200,000 men and 300 triremes under the satrap Pharnabazus, with the Athenian Iphicrates leading the Greek mercenaries. They landed at the Mendesian mouth and took a fort, but Pharnabazus refused Iphicrates' plan to rush Memphis, the two fell out, the Nile flood rose, and the army re-embarked and left. It was the high-water mark of the last native Egyptian state.
entries.note: Diodorus 15.41–43; Cornelius Nepos, Iphicrates 2. John Ray in Cambridge Ancient History VI (1994) ch.4; Lloyd in Shaw (2000) pp.378–79.

entries.label: The reconquest of 343 and Alexander's arrival
entries.hint: Artaxerxes III's third invasion, in 343, broke through: Greek mercenary generals on the Persian side outmanoeuvred Nectanebo II's forward defence, the frontier towns fell, and the last pharaoh withdrew south and vanished. Persia held Egypt for eleven bitter years, its temples looted and its walls slighted. When Alexander the Great reached the frontier in 332, the Persian satrap Mazaces, left without an army after Issus, simply handed the country over; Alexander was welcomed as a liberator.
entries.note: Diodorus 16.40–51; [Aristotle] Oeconomica 2.2.33–35; Arrian, Anabasis 3.1. The looting of temples and records: the Satrap Stela (Cairo CG 22182) and Ptolemaic tradition. Briant (2002) pp.685–90.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Saite reform of the state, Demotic administration, the Persian satrapy, and the temple as the surviving institution

entries.label: The Saite reconstruction of the state
entries.hint: Psamtik I and his successors rebuilt a single Egyptian state out of a century and a half of fragments, run from Sais in the western Delta. They maintained a standing army of two elements — a native warrior class (the machimoi of Greek writers) settled on hereditary land allotments, and paid Greek and Carian mercenary corps garrisoning the three frontiers at Daphnae in the east, Elephantine in the south and Marea in the west — plus a war fleet on the Greek model.
entries.note: Herodotus 2.30, 2.154, 2.163–68 (the warrior class and the garrisons). Analysis: Alan B. Lloyd, 'The Late Period', in Shaw (ed.), Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) pp.369–94; Damien Agut-Labordère, 'The Saite Period', in Moreno García (ed.), Ancient Egyptian Administration (2013).

entries.label: Demotic and the paperwork state
entries.hint: From about the mid-seventh century a new cursive script and its own form of the spoken language, which Egyptologists call Demotic, spread out of the Delta and displaced the older business hand across the country. With it came a denser documentary culture: standardised sale and lease contracts, marriage settlements, tax receipts, temple ledgers and private letters, all in a form quick to write and read. Egyptian administration and private law became, for the first time, thoroughly paper-based.
entries.note: Mark Depauw, A Companion to Demotic Studies (1997); Janet Johnson (ed.), Life in a Multi-Cultural Society: Egypt from Cambyses to Constantine (1992). The transition from 'abnormal hieratic': Koenraad Donker van Heel, Abnormal Hieratic and Early Demotic Texts (1995).

entries.label: The law of Egypt codified
entries.hint: Darius I ordered a commission of Egyptian priests, soldiers and scribes to write down 'the law of Egypt' as it had stood down to the reign of Amasis — temple regulations, and public and private law — a project said to have taken sixteen years and to have been issued in Aramaic and Demotic versions. It reflects a wider Late Period reality: Egyptian family and property law, worked out in Demotic contracts and temple courts, kept running under Persian, and later Ptolemaic and Roman, sovereignty.
entries.note: The codification: verso of the Demotic Chronicle (P. BN 215); Nicolas Grimal, A History of Ancient Egypt (1992) pp.372–73. Late Period legal practice: Schafik Allam, and the Demotic legal manuals such as the Hermopolis Legal Code (P. Cairo 30602 etc.).

entries.label: Egypt as a Persian satrapy
entries.hint: Under Persia, Egypt (with Cyrenaica and Libya) was the empire's sixth satrapy, assessed by Herodotus at 700 talents of silver a year plus the revenue of Lake Moeris's fishery and grain for 120,000 troops in the country. A satrap resided at Memphis; Aramaic was the chancery language; Persian and local officials shared the courts; and the royal courier road was extended to the Nile. It was a rich province governed, most of the time, at arm's length.
entries.note: Herodotus 3.90–91. Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002) pp.472–84, 588–91; Melanie Wasmuth, Ägypto-persische Herrscher- und Herrschaftspräsentation in der Achämenidenzeit (2017).

entries.label: The temple as the enduring institution
entries.hint: Across five changes of regime in three centuries — Saite, Persian, the last native kings, Persian again, Macedonian — the one continuous Egyptian institution was the temple. Its estates, granaries, courts, workshops and hereditary priesthoods carried on; every incoming ruler, Egyptian or foreign, sought legitimacy by endowing it, restoring its buildings, and being named in its daily ritual as the reigning king. The temple was where 'Egypt' persisted between dynasties.
entries.note: Christopher Eyre, The Use of Documents in Pharaonic Egypt (2013); Damien Agut-Labordère, 'Le statut économique des temples égyptiens à l'époque perse', in Baslez & Munnich (eds.), various. The Satrap Stela (Cairo CG 22182) shows the pattern under Ptolemy.

entries.label: The Petition of Peteese
entries.hint: A Demotic papyrus, over two metres long, records a Middle Egyptian priest's account of his family's century-long feud with a rival clan over shares of the priesthood and its income at the temple of Teudjoi — beatings, a temple burned, appeals carried to the chief of the fleet and the king's agents, verdicts won and then ignored. It is the fullest surviving picture of how an ordinary Egyptian tried to use, and was ground down by, the Saite and early Persian legal system.
entries.note: Papyrus Rylands 9: Günter Vittmann, Der demotische Papyrus Rylands 9 (1998); F.Ll. Griffith, Catalogue of the Demotic Papyri in the John Rylands Library (1909). Analysis: Koenraad Donker van Heel, and Kim Ryholt, 'The Turin King-List', on the milieu.

entries.label: The decree stelae of the last native kings
entries.hint: The Thirtieth Dynasty used the carved royal decree at temple gates as an instrument of rule. Nectanebo I's near-identical stelae at Naukratis and the port of Thonis-Heracleion assign to the temple of the goddess Neith at Sais a tenth of the customs duty on imports and of the tax on locally made goods passing through those Greek-facing ports — a king directing trade revenue to the national goddess and, in the same act, advertising royal control of the foreign traffic.
entries.note: Naukratis Stela (Cairo JE 34002) and the twin Thonis-Heracleion Stela: Christophe Thiers, La stèle de Ptolémée VIII... and, for the Nectanebo pair, Anne-Sophie von Bomhard, The Decree of Sais (2012). Underwater find at Thonis: Franck Goddio, 2000.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Archaising temple religion, the industrial-scale animal cults, and the Egyptian gods enter the Greek world

entries.label: The archaising renaissance of religion
entries.hint: The Saite period consciously reached back over a thousand years to reconstruct 'correct' religion: Old and Middle Kingdom texts were dug out and recopied, temple liturgy was fixed and standardised, priestly titles and the order of the gods were regularised, and the goddess Neith of Sais was raised to the head of the pantheon as a primeval creator. It was less a new theology than an editorial project — canonising a tradition felt to have drifted during the centuries of division.
entries.note: Peter Der Manuelian, Living in the Past: Studies in Archaism of the Egyptian Twenty-Sixth Dynasty (1994). Neith at Sais: Ramadan el-Sayed, La déesse Neith de Saïs (1982). Herodotus 2.59, 2.62, 2.169–71 on the Sais temple.

entries.label: The animal cults industrialised
entries.hint: In the Late Period the votive burial of sacred animals became a mass industry. Temple-run establishments bred, killed, mummified and interred them by the million: ibises and falcons in the vast catacombs at Saqqara, Tuna el-Gebel and Abydos, cats at the Bubasteion, dogs at Saqqara, cows as 'Mothers of Apis'. A worshipper paid for an animal to be mummified and buried as a messenger carrying a prayer to its god — a devotional transaction available to anyone with a little silver.
entries.note: Sacred Animal Necropolis, North Saqqara: H.S. Smith, A Visit to Ancient Egypt (1974); the EES excavations. Tuna el-Gebel ibises: Dieter Kessler. Overview: Salima Ikram (ed.), Divine Creatures: Animal Mummies in Ancient Egypt (2005).

entries.label: The Apis and the Serapeum
entries.hint: The Apis bull of Memphis — one living animal at a time, the herald of Ptah — reached its cultic peak now. Each Apis was given a state funeral, embalmed by a ritual set out in its own papyrus, and entombed in a granite sarcophagus of up to seventy tonnes in the enlarged galleries of the Serapeum, its burial dated by a stela. In death the bull was Osiris-Apis, and it was this Memphite Osiris-Apis that the first Ptolemy would refashion into the Greek-Egyptian god Serapis.
entries.note: Auguste Mariette, Le Sérapéum de Memphis (1857–66); the Apis stelae, Malinine, Posener & Vercoutter, Catalogue des stèles du Sérapéum (1968). The Apis Embalming Ritual: Papyrus Vindob. 3873, R.L. Vos (1993).

entries.label: Osiris and the Late Period afterlife
entries.hint: Osiris religion filled the period. The Khoiak festival re-enacted the god's death and revival every year, with 'corn mummies' — moulded figures of soil and grain that sprouted — buried in miniature coffins. Dozens of small Osiris chapels went up around Karnak, several endowed by the God's Wives. Ordinary funerary equipment settled into a Late Period standard: a fixed 'Saite recension' Book of the Dead of some 165 numbered chapters, stone sarcophagi with underworld texts, and sets of 401 blue faience shabti workers.
entries.note: Khoiak and corn mummies: Maria Centrone, and the Osiris chapels of Karnak, Claude Traunecker et al. Saite Book of the Dead recension: Malcolm Mosher, 'The Ancient Egyptian Book of the Dead in the Late Period', in various; shabti sets, Jacques-F. Aubert, Statuettes égyptiennes (1974).

entries.label: The Egyptian gods enter the Greek world
entries.hint: Contact ran both ways. Greeks at Naukratis built sanctuaries but also dedicated to Egyptian gods; the oracle of Amun at Siwa, which the Greeks called Ammon, was consulted by Sparta, Athens and Cyrene and would famously receive Alexander; Herodotus systematically matched Egyptian gods to Greek ones (Amun–Zeus, Osiris–Dionysus, Neith–Athena); and the first cults of Isis outside Egypt, served by Egyptian residents, appeared in the port of Piraeus in the fourth century.
entries.note: Herodotus 2.42–64. Siwa oracle: Herodotus 1.46, 2.32–33; Arrian 3.3–4. Isis at Piraeus: IG II² 337 (333/2 BC). Ian Rutherford (ed.), Greco-Egyptian Interactions (2016).

entries.label: The healing statue and the Metternich Stela
entries.hint: Late Period Egyptians met danger — scorpion sting, snakebite, fever, the evil eye — with dense magical texts on stone. Small 'cippi of Horus' showing the child god gripping serpents and scorpions, and larger 'healing statues' covered head to foot in spells, were set up in temple courts; water poured over the inscriptions was collected and drunk or washed with, transferring the protection. The Metternich Stela, made under Nectanebo II, is the most elaborate surviving example.
entries.note: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum 50.85), commissioned by the priest Esatum/Nespakashuty under Nectanebo II. Healing statues: Heike Sternberg-el Hotabi, Untersuchungen zur Überlieferungsgeschichte der Horusstelen (1999); the Djedhor statue from Athribis (Cairo JE 46341).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Saite revival of Old Kingdom art, hard-stone sculpture, the last great native temples, and Demotic literature

entries.label: The Saite revival of Old Kingdom art
entries.hint: Saite artists studied thous-year-old monuments and copied them. Relief in the vast Asasif tomb-chapels of the stewards Ibi and Pabasa reproduces, scene for scene, agricultural and daily-life compositions from Sixth-Dynasty tombs at Saqqara — in one case the copyists' guide-grid and errors show them working from a pattern. Statuary revived Old and Middle Kingdom facial types and the smooth, closed forms of the pyramid age, finished to a high polish: the 'Saite renaissance' in stone.
entries.note: Peter Der Manuelian, Living in the Past: Studies in Archaism of the Egyptian Twenty-Sixth Dynasty (1994); Edna R. Russmann, 'Aspects of Egyptian Art: Archaism', in Egyptian Sculpture: Cairo and Luxor (1989). Tomb of Ibi (TT36): Kuhlmann & Schenkel (1983).

entries.label: Hard-stone sculpture at its technical peak
entries.hint: Late Period sculptors achieved an unmatched command of the hardest stones — greywacke, schist, basalt, granodiorite — carving crisp detail and mirror-smooth surfaces without iron tools. The characteristic products are the cube-shaped 'block statue', and figures of officials holding a shrine or a divine emblem, their back-pillars and skirts covered with autobiography and prayer. The finest heads, like the anonymous green schist 'Berlin Green Head', combine idealised smoothness with sharply individual features.
entries.note: Berlin Green Head (Ägyptisches Museum 12500). Bernard Bothmer, Egyptian Sculpture of the Late Period, 700 B.C. to A.D. 100 (1960) is the foundational catalogue. Regine Schulz, Die Entwicklung und Bedeutung des kuboiden Statuentypus (1992).

entries.label: The last great native temples
entries.hint: The Thirtieth Dynasty ran a temple-building programme larger than any since Ramesses II, and its plans set the template the Ptolemies would follow for two more centuries. Nectanebo I began the Isis temple complex on the island of Philae and the granite Iseum at Behbeit el-Hagar; Nectanebo I and II added the great first pylon and the sphinx avenue at Karnak, kiosks, birth-houses (mammisis) and gateways across the country — the classic Egyptian temple in its final, fully standardised form.
entries.note: Philae: Gerhard Haeny and the UNESCO relocation documentation. Behbeit el-Hagar: Christine Favard-Meeks, Le temple de Behbeit el-Hagara (1991). Thirtieth-Dynasty building overview: Dieter Arnold, Temples of the Last Pharaohs (1999).

entries.label: The monolithic naos
entries.hint: A signature Late Period object is the naos — the shrine that held a temple's cult image — carved from a single huge block of hard stone and covered with reliefs. Nectanebo I's naoi at Saft el-Hinna and Mendes are among the largest ever made. The most remarkable, the 'Naos of the Decades' from Bubastis, maps the thirty-six ten-day divisions of the year onto decan stars and to periods of danger and safety — a calendar of fortune cut in granite.
entries.note: Naos of the Decades (Louvre D 37 + Greco-Roman Museum, Alexandria + Aboukir Bay fragments): Anne-Sophie von Bomhard, The Naos of the Decades (2008). Saft el-Hinna naos (Cairo): Édouard Naville, The Shrine of Saft el Henneh (1887).

entries.label: Demotic literature
entries.hint: A body of literature grew up in the Demotic script and language. There are cycles of heroic tales — the wars of Inaros's descendants, the priest-magicians of the Setne stories — and animal fables; wisdom in the pointed one-line proverbs of the Instruction of Ankhsheshonq and the meditative Papyrus Insinger; and the 'Demotic Chronicle', a set of cryptic oracular verses read as commentary on the succession of kings and the promise of a native saviour after foreign rule.
entries.note: Demotic Chronicle: P. BN 215; Johannes Dieleman and the translation history. Setne and Inaros cycles: Kim Ryholt, The Carlsberg Papyri and Narrative Literature from the Tebtunis Temple Library (2012). Ankhsheshonq: P. BM 10508. Most manuscripts are Ptolemaic copies of Late Period compositions.

entries.label: The bronze votive figure
entries.hint: Temple foundries turned out small bronze figures of the gods — a striding Osiris, Isis nursing the child Horus, the cat-goddess Bastet, Neith, the Apis bull — by the tens of thousands, cast from moulds around a fired clay core. Worshippers bought and dedicated them; temples buried the accumulation in favissae. They are the most common surviving Egyptian antiquity, and the clearest sign of a devotional economy in which anyone could leave a permanent offering.
entries.note: Marsha Hill & Deborah Schorsch (eds.), Gifts for the Gods: Images from Egyptian Temples (2007); Günther Roeder, Ägyptische Bronzefiguren (1956). The North Saqqara bronze hoards: G.T. Martin and the EES.

entries.label: Temple music and the arriving aulos
entries.hint: The temple choirs and the office of 'chantress' carried on from the Third Intermediate Period, now supplying the music for an ever-busier calendar of festivals and processions, with the arched harp, round frame drum, sistrum and double reed-pipe. At Naukratis and in the mercenary towns, Greek music — the paired auloi, the lyre, drinking songs — was played alongside, one of many small cultural imports that arrived with the Greek presence.
entries.note: Lise Manniche, Music and Musicians in Ancient Egypt (1991); Suzanne Onstine, The Role of the Chantress (2005). Greek instruments at Naukratis: the votive material in Alexandra Villing et al., Naukratis: Greeks in Egypt (British Museum online catalogue).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Herodotus in Egypt, the House of Life, Demotic wisdom and law, and Greek philosophers at Naukratis

entries.label: Herodotus in Egypt
entries.hint: Herodotus of Halicarnassus toured Persian-ruled Egypt around 450 and devoted the whole second book of his Histories to it: the land as 'the gift of the river', competing explanations of the summer flood, the claim that Egypt was the oldest of nations and that Greece had taken its gods, festivals and geometry from it, and pages of custom relayed from priest-informants. Much of it is garbled or wrong, but it is the founding text both of the Greek image of Egypt and of Western descriptive ethnography.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories Book II. Commentary: Alan B. Lloyd, Herodotus Book II, 3 vols. (1975–88). On the reliability question: Ian Moyer, Egypt and the Limits of Hellenism (2011) pp.42–83.

entries.label: The House of Life and the priestly sciences
entries.hint: With the palace weak or foreign, formal learning lived in the temple 'House of Life' — the scriptorium and school attached to major sanctuaries, where priests copied and composed the texts of ritual, medicine, astronomy, dream interpretation, magic and temple law, and taught the hieroglyphic and hieratic scripts now needed only by specialists. Herodotus's informants, Udjahorresnet the 'chief physician', and the compilers of Darius's law code all belonged to this world.
entries.note: Alan Gardiner, 'The House of Life', JEA 24 (1938). Udjahorresnet as 'chief physician' and House-of-Life restorer: Lloyd, JEA 68 (1982). Kim Ryholt & Gojko Barjamovic (eds.), Libraries before Alexandria (2019).

entries.label: Demotic wisdom and the doctrine of fate
entries.hint: Late Period wisdom literature is more resigned and more individual than the classic instructions. The Instruction of Ankhsheshonq offers hundreds of blunt, sometimes contradictory one-line maxims on getting by. Papyrus Insinger organises its teaching thematically around the idea that a person's character and lot are ultimately set by the god and by fate (shai), and that wisdom lies in accepting this. It marks a turn toward a providential, almost philosophical, ethics.
entries.note: Instruction of Ankhsheshonq: P. BM 10508; Miriam Lichtheim, Late Egyptian Wisdom Literature in the International Context (1983). Papyrus Insinger (Leiden): translation in Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature III (1980) pp.184–217.

entries.label: Egyptian doctors and the Greeks
entries.hint: Egyptian medicine had an international reputation. Herodotus reports that the Persian kings Cyrus and Darius kept Egyptian physicians at court, and that in Egypt medicine was minutely specialised — 'each physician treats one disease and no more'. Egyptian drug lore, surgical practice and the temple sanatorium (where the sick slept hoping for a healing dream) fed into the Greek medical tradition just as it was forming around Hippocrates.
entries.note: Herodotus 2.84, 3.1, 3.129–30. Udjahorresnet's medical title: Lloyd, JEA 68 (1982). John Nunn, Ancient Egyptian Medicine (1996) pp.204–06 on the Egyptian–Greek transmission; Heinrich von Staden, Herophilus (1989) on the Alexandrian sequel.

entries.label: The decans, the calendar and fortune
entries.hint: Late Period astronomy kept refining the old apparatus — decan-star lists, the 'Book of Nut' on the sky-goddess and the stars' risings, tables aligning the 365-day civil calendar with the 25-year lunar cycle — while the civil year still drifted a day every four years for want of a leap day. The Naos of the Decades fused this astronomy with astrology: each ten-day decan governs a stretch of the year and brings sickness or safety, an early Egyptian step toward a horoscopic view of time.
entries.note: Otto Neugebauer & Richard Parker, Egyptian Astronomical Texts, 3 vols. (1960–69). Naos of the Decades: von Bomhard, The Naos of the Decades (2008). The wandering calendar and the (rejected) Canopus reform of 238 BC lie just beyond this folio.
